items.questionAndWhy: Can a chatbot-delivered positive-psychology program strengthen existing friendships and wellbeing, rather than simply engaging isolated individuals? The distinction tests whether social context changes intervention outcomes.
items.whatTheyDid: Turóczi and colleagues preregistered a six-week PERMA-based chatbot program delivered through existing friendship dyads and groups. Friendship clusters were randomized to intervention or waitlist; the final analysis included 251 young adults (124 intervention, 127 control). Measures included PERMA dimensions, friendship support, loneliness and closeness.
items.whatTheyFound: The intervention group reported higher postintervention friend support and higher relationship and accomplishment scores. Closeness increased within the intervention arm. There were no significant intervention effects for overall wellbeing, loneliness, positive emotion, engagement or meaning. Outcomes were self-reported, follow-up was short, and the design does not isolate chatbot content from group participation.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX practitioner and community interventions could test whether existing social relationships change the impact of structured exercises. Evaluate relational outcomes separately from broad wellbeing; do not describe this as a general-purpose mental-health effect. Transfer to operational team cohesion or influence work is untested.
items.streamTitle: Friendship-based chatbot intervention improved relational outcomes but not overall wellbeing
items.streamSummary: A preregistered cluster RCT (251 young adults) found a six-week chatbot program for existing friendship groups improved perceived friend support and selected PERMA dimensions, but not overall wellbeing or loneliness.
items.attribution: Turóczi, Szabó, Verebélyi et al. — Scientific Reports (preregistered cluster randomized trial; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does making another person's face resemble the viewer reliably increase liking during a conversational interaction? The hypothesis matters for digital identity cues and how social similarity is operationalized.
items.whatTheyDid: Kasahara, Claggett and Shirado preregistered an online yoked-stimulus experiment. Sixty participants saw eight two-person conversation videos in which a speaker's face was morphed toward their own or another participant's face, yielding 480 evaluations; matched control viewers helped separate self-relevance from visual morphing artifacts.
items.whatTheyFound: Greater self-resemblance did not consistently increase positive evaluations. Exploratory analyses suggested higher-self-esteem viewers evaluated self-resembling speakers more favorably, while lower-self-esteem viewers sometimes showed the opposite pattern. Those moderator analyses were exploratory, and the 60-person online sample limits precision and transfer to natural encounters.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX social-perception studies should not assume appearance similarity produces a universal affiliation effect. Test self-concept and actual interaction context rather than rely on facial morphs as a generic influence tool. Neither persuasive effects nor real-world relationship formation was evaluated.
items.streamTitle: Facial self-resemblance did not reliably make conversational partners more likable
items.streamSummary: A preregistered 60-person, yoked-video experiment found no general liking benefit from self-resembling faces. Exploratory self-esteem differences suggest heterogeneity, not a confirmed universal social-bonding mechanism.
items.attribution: Kasahara, Claggett and Shirado — Scientific Reports (preregistered online social-perception experiment; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How is reported AI-tool use related to procrastination in students, and do anxiety, self-control or guilt change that association? This concerns self-regulation, not just whether AI improves task efficiency.
items.whatTheyDid: Wu and Zhou surveyed 782 students at two convenience-selected public universities in Guangxi, China. They measured AI usage, academic procrastination, anxiety, self-control and AI-related guilt and fitted cross-sectional mediation and moderated-mediation models.
items.whatTheyFound: More AI use was associated with more procrastination. Standardized indirect associations through anxiety and self-control were 0.129 and 0.119, together accounting for about 54.87% of the total modeled association. At higher AI guilt, both the positive use–anxiety and negative use–self-control associations were weaker. The same-time self-reports cannot determine whether AI use causes procrastination or vice versa.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX AI-assisted education should measure task initiation, independent completion, stress and self-regulation rather than infer benefits from usage alone. These are candidate pathways for prospective tests, not demonstrated causal mediators or evidence about working professionals.
items.streamTitle: AI use and academic procrastination were associated through anxiety and self-control
items.streamSummary: A cross-sectional survey of 782 Chinese university students linked AI use with procrastination and modeled indirect associations through anxiety and self-control; simultaneous self-reports prohibit causal conclusions.
items.attribution: Wu and Zhou — Scientific Reports (cross-sectional university survey; November 20, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How have Russian information operations in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania used historical memory, language and minority identity in wider strategic competition? A key analytical challenge is separating narratives, distribution networks and observable effects.
items.whatTheyDid: List, Person and Phelps produced an October 28 Foreign Policy Research Institute historical and strategic report synthesizing events and information activity in the Baltic states over roughly two decades, including the 2007 Estonian Bronze Soldier controversy, cultural organizations, conventional media and online channels.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors argue that Russian state-linked efforts increasingly combine historical revisionism, identity grievances and organizational networks to challenge Baltic and NATO cohesion. This is a documented strategic interpretation of historical and open-source evidence, not an experiment measuring how many people changed beliefs or a causal assessment of specific campaigns.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX OIE case studies, code identity grievance, historical referent, organizational carrier, platform amplification and observable audience outcomes separately. Use competing explanations for major political events; the report's strategic interpretation does not itself quantify campaign effectiveness.
items.streamTitle: Baltic information-war review traced identity grievances across organizations and media channels
items.streamSummary: An October 28 FPRI report traces Russian information activity in the Baltic states through historical-memory disputes, identity narratives and state-linked organizations. It offers a strategic case framework, not causal persuasion estimates.
items.attribution: Briana List, Robert Person and Reagan Phelps — Foreign Policy Research Institute (historical strategic report; October 28, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Will AI assistants preserve established factual answers when challenged by users, and can they evaluate new evidence and policy interactions across languages? Reliable knowledge mediation is more demanding than recalling an accepted fact.
items.whatTheyDid: An original UNESCO–UCL report, summarized in UNESCO's November 16 release updated November 18, tested up to 33 language models across nine climate and environmental datasets and 13 languages. Fifteen models were evaluated for factual deference under user disagreement; 656 policy questions were checked against En-ROADS simulation references.
items.whatTheyFound: The official summary reports roughly 90% accuracy on neutral climate facts, but eight in ten tested responses pivoted at the first mild challenge. English accuracy averaged 88.6% versus 78.3% in Swahili. Policy-interaction reasoning achieved 33.8% in a three-choice test, near 33.3% chance. Results concern selected model versions, climate questions and benchmark definitions, not all future assistants or policy decisions.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX AI research workflows should test answer stability under user disagreement, evidence interpretation and language changes independently from ordinary factual recall. The climate domain supplies a concrete stress-test template; accuracy rates should not be generalized to other research topics without testing.
items.streamTitle: UNESCO–UCL found AI systems vulnerable to user pushback and multilingual reasoning gaps
items.streamSummary: UNESCO–UCL tests of up to 33 models found frequent agreement with incorrect user challenges, uneven accuracy across 13 languages and near-chance policy-interaction judgments. These are climate-domain AI benchmarks, not observed human belief effects.
items.attribution: UNESCO and University College London — Can We Trust AI on Climate? (original report; UNESCO release November 16, updated November 18, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do simulated echo chambers change when agents share underlying beliefs as well as expressed opinions? Models limited to opinion averages may omit the belief structures that make positions mutually reinforcing.
items.whatTheyDid: Kataoka, Euzenat and Hasebe extended an opinion-dynamics simulation with belief-merging operations and value-guided coherence constraints. They varied starting conditions and tolerance and measured homogeneity, segregation and reinforcement for beliefs and opinions.
items.whatTheyFound: Under the chosen simulation rules, echo chambers occurred when beliefs propagated, and enforcing coherence between beliefs and opinions produced more belief echo chambers with fewer agents in each. This is a formal simulation comparison; it did not measure actual online communities or establish that the hypothesized belief-updating rules are psychologically accurate.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX FCM or ABM designs could explicitly test whether multiple interdependent beliefs yield different fragmentation predictions than a single opinion variable. Validate the coupling assumptions against observed longitudinal belief networks before drawing conclusions about real polarization or intervention effects.
items.streamTitle: Belief–opinion coupling changed modeled echo-chamber formation
items.streamSummary: A November 19 preprint found opinion–belief coherence created more but smaller simulated belief echo chambers under specified tolerance and updating rules. It is a model result, not observed social polarization.
items.attribution: Kataoka, Euzenat and Hasebe — arXiv preprint (formal opinion/belief simulation; November 19, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can causal-event statements distributed across different social-media posts be linked more accurately than by treating each post alone? This matters for reconstructing reported event sequences from fragmented information streams.
items.whatTheyDid: Duong and colleagues proposed STAGE, using local event-causality seeds to retrieve related cross-tweet occurrences, weakly label event pairs, and train a spatiotemporal graph-attention model. It was evaluated on California wildfire and Hurricane Harvey posts against human-labeled cross-tweet tests and 15 baselines.
items.whatTheyFound: Cross-post supervision increased AUPRC by 0.340 on the wildfire set and 0.107 on Hurricane Harvey relative to local-only supervision; in-domain AUROC reached 0.885 and 0.710 respectively. Transfer between disasters was asymmetric. The task predicts annotated causal-event relations in text, not scientifically identified intervention effects.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX information-event mapping could use candidate cross-source event links to guide analyst review of event chains. Treat extracted causal language as a hypothesis requiring independent evidence, especially across settings where event distributions differ. Do not use classifier scores as proof of actual causal mechanisms.
items.streamTitle: Cross-post event linking improved causal-relation classification in fragmented social reports
items.streamSummary: STAGE combined weak cross-tweet supervision and spatiotemporal graphs, improving event-relation classification on wildfire and hurricane tweets, with asymmetric transfer. It detects reported causal links, not intervention causality.
items.attribution: Duong, Gary, Levin and Nguyen — arXiv preprint (cross-tweet event-relation benchmark; November 19, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can researchers compare party positions on economic and cultural dimensions across countries and decades without conflating heterogeneous text counts and expert survey judgments? A common longitudinal scale is needed for contextual political-information analysis.
items.whatTheyDid: Seimel released an election-year panel covering 708 parties in 65 countries from 1944–2025. A Bayesian dynamic item-response model combines manifesto, media and expert evidence on economic left–right and cosmopolitan–traditionalist dimensions, with posterior uncertainty and held-out, robustness and convergence checks.
items.whatTheyFound: The publication provides harmonized historical estimates and uncertainty for party-election observations, plus methodological validation checks. These are model-based party positions, not directly observed individual ideology, voter motives or causal responses to communications. Comparability depends on source coverage and model assumptions.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX cross-national information-environment research can use the panel as a time-varying political context layer, keeping posterior uncertainty and source composition visible. It should not be used as a proxy for population psychology or as evidence that particular messages caused opinion change.
items.streamTitle: Open longitudinal party-position panel integrates text and expert judgments with uncertainty
items.streamSummary: A November 21 Scientific Data release provides Bayesian economic/cultural position estimates for 708 parties in 65 countries across 1944–2025, integrating text and experts with uncertainty. It is contextual data infrastructure, not voter-level measurement.
items.attribution: Armin Seimel — Scientific Data (cross-national party-position dataset descriptor; November 21, 2026)
